title: No Cell Signal? No Problem: The First Satellite Dog Collar Is Here
summary:
Picture this: you're deep in a national forest, miles from the nearest town, when your dog suddenly takes off after a squirrel. Your heart sinks as you glance at your phone — zero bars. That gut-wrenching scenario is exactly why Fi developed the world's first satellite-connected dog collar, which went live on July 8.

The Fi Ultra Direct-to-Cell tracker combines a GPS receiver with a modem that normally talks to T-Mobile's cellular network. But when there's no tower in reach, it automatically switches to SpaceX's Starlink satellites. The collar pings a satellite passing overhead, which relays your dog's coordinates to the Fi app on your phone. You can also draw a geofence — a virtual boundary — around your yard. The moment your dog crosses it, you get an alert.

Fi founder Jonathan Bensamoun originally created GPS trackers to monitor his German shepherd, Thor, and ensure his dog walker wasn't slacking. But the number-one complaint from customers was always the same: the device was useless where cell coverage was spotty. When Starlink began beaming connectivity directly to smartphones in 2024, Bensamoun saw the solution. "The number one complaint from customers is either 'I live in an area where the cellular network is not really good' or 'I get really worried about my dog when it's away from the typical suburban area,'" he told Space.com.

Beyond location tracking, the collar can send short bursts of vibrations or sounds to your dog. With training — rewarding your pup with a treat every time the vibration goes off — they'll learn to associate the buzz with food waiting at home. That means they might come running back on their own, no shouting required. The battery lasts multiple days, crucial when a search stretches on.

GPS tracking for animals isn't new; scientists first strapped clunky devices onto moose and caribou in the 1990s. But only in the early 2010s did the tech shrink enough for pets. Today, about 11 million dogs worldwide wear some form of GPS tracker. Fi's innovation takes it a leap further, offering what Bensamoun calls "nearly omnipresent connectivity." For anyone who's ever frantically searched for a lost dog in the backcountry, that's a game-changer.
why_it_matters: For adventurous families who camp or hike with their dogs, this technology could mean the difference between a quick reunion and a tragic loss; it also marks a turning point where satellite connectivity becomes a normal part of everyday consumer gadgets.

background_read: For decades, satellite tracking was reserved for ocean liners, military vehicles, and large wildlife like polar bears. It took the miniaturization of electronics and the rise of smartphone components to make GPS collars light enough for pets.

SpaceX's Starlink constellation (a project by the aerospace company founded by Elon Musk), which began beaming direct signals to ordinary smartphones in 2024, changed the game. Previously, a pet tracker needed to be within range of a cell tower, leaving remote hikers helpless if their dog bolted.

Fi (a New York-based pet technology company) was founded by Jonathan Bensamoun, who originally built a GPS tracker for his own German shepherd, Thor. The company already had a popular cellular-based collar, but constant customer complaints about dead zones pushed him to add satellite connectivity.
The concept of using vibrations to guide a dog draws on behavioral training methods used by police and hunting dogs; the collar becomes a long-distance recall cue.

perspectives.description: Pet owners and animal rescue groups applaud the safety net — dogs can be located even in deep wilderness, reducing stress and search costs.

Privacy advocates worry that always-on location tracking could be exploited by hackers, or that neighbors might misuse geofence data. Also, the collar's cost may put it out of reach for lower-income families.

The collar is part of a broader trend where satellite internet is transforming industries from shipping to outdoor recreation. Its success depends on Starlink's continued expansion and regulatory approval in every country.
Future versions could integrate health monitoring (heart rate, temperature) or serve as training hubs, but this raises questions about how much data collection is too much for a simple pet accessory.
